backlog.spec: Swap the SVR head in train.py for exact Gaussian process regression on the same 0.5 Tanimoto / 0.5 descriptor-RBF precomputed kernel, which gives a smooth posterior mean rather than a sparse epsilon-insensitive fit. Implement it directly with numpy rather than sklearn's GaussianProcessRegressor: solve (K_train + lam * I) alpha = y_centered with scipy.linalg.cho_factor / cho_solve, then predict K_test @ alpha + y_mean, where y is the current rank-normalized, mean-centred, sd-scaled target. Choose the noise level lam by maximizing the log marginal likelihood -0.5 * y' alpha - 0.5 * logdet(K + lam I) - 0.5 n log(2 pi) over lam in a log grid np.logspace(-3, 0, 13); the Cholesky factor gives logdet from the diagonal, so all 13 candidates cost one 970x970 factorization each and the whole fit stays well under a second. Keep featurization, descriptors and the kernel mix exactly as they are.
backlog.title: Gaussian process regression with the existing mixed kernel

backlog.spec: In the current train.py the two kernels are combined with fixed weights (0.5 * tanimoto + 0.5 * rbf) and the RBF bandwidth is fixed at gamma = 1/n_descriptors. Replace both constants with a small joint inner search. Precompute the Tanimoto kernel once and the squared-distance matrix of the standardized descriptors once (train-train and test-train), then form rbf = exp(-g * sq) for g in {0.1, 0.3, 1.0, 3.0} times the base 1/n_descriptors, and mixing weight w in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} so K = (1-w)*tanimoto + w*rbf. Evaluate each of the 12 (g, w) pairs by 4-fold KFold(shuffle=True, random_state=seed) inner CV on the training rows, slicing the precomputed kernels with np.ix_, scoring out-of-fold Spearman with the current SVR settings (C=5.0, epsilon=0.05). Refit on the full training kernel with the winning pair and predict. Reusing the cached squared-distance matrix is what keeps this fast; do not recompute descriptors or fingerprints inside the loop.
backlog.title: Joint inner-CV of descriptor gamma and kernel mixing weight

backlog.spec: Keep the current kernel SVR exactly as it is, and add a second model: a LightGBM regressor (lgb.LGBMRegressor, n_estimators=600, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=15, min_child_samples=10, subsample=0.8, subsample_freq=1, colsample_bytree=0.5, reg_lambda=1.0, random_state=seed, n_jobs=8, verbose=-1) trained on the horizontal concatenation of the binary Morgan bits and the standardized descriptor matrix, with the same rank-transformed target. Convert each model's test predictions to ranks with scipy.stats.rankdata, scale to [0,1] by dividing by the number of test molecules, and return the simple average of the two rank vectors. Rank averaging is safe here because the loss is Spearman-based.
backlog.title: Average SVR with a LightGBM model on descriptors plus fingerprints

backlog.spec: The descriptor RBF currently uses a single fixed gamma = 1/n_features on all ~210 standardized RDKit descriptors, which may be badly scaled. Replace this with a gamma chosen by the median heuristic: compute the median of the pairwise squared Euclidean distances among training descriptor rows (subsample up to 400 rows for speed) and set gamma = 1.0 / median_sq_dist, then additionally sweep a multiplier in {0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0} using an inner 5-fold KFold(shuffle=True, random_state=seed) scored by Spearman, keeping the 0.5/0.5 kernel mix and SVR settings fixed. Use the selected gamma for both K_train and K_test.
backlog.title: Per-block descriptor RBF with tuned gamma

backlog.spec: Hepatocyte clearance values are strongly right-skewed, and the current code discards all magnitude information by replacing y with its uniform ranks. Replace the rank transform with y = np.log10(np.clip(y, a_min=small_positive, a_max=None)) where small_positive is half the smallest positive training value, then standardize to zero mean and unit variance before fitting. Keep the kernel construction and SVR(C=5.0, epsilon=0.05) unchanged and return the raw decision values (Spearman is invariant to the monotone back-transform, so no inversion is needed). This tests whether magnitude information helps the SVR place its support vectors better than pure ranks.
backlog.title: Log-transformed target in place of rank transform

backlog.spec: Replace the single SVR fit in train.py with a bag of 15 SVRs, each trained on a random 70% subsample of the training molecules, and average their test predictions after converting each member's predictions to ranks. Use np.random.default_rng(seed) to draw the subsamples (without replacement, so each member sees about 679 of 970 molecules), slice the precomputed combined training kernel with np.ix_ for the member's rows and columns, slice K_test columns to the same training subset, and keep C=5.0, epsilon=0.05 and the rank-normalized z-scored target as they are (recompute the target mean/sd within each subsample). Convert each member's test predictions with scipy.stats.rankdata, divide by the number of test molecules, and return the mean across the 15 members. Because the loss is 1 minus Spearman, rank averaging rather than value averaging is the right pooling rule, and bagging decorrelates the errors of a model whose kernel is dominated by a few high-similarity pairs.
backlog.title: Bagged SVRs on 70% subsamples with rank averaging

backlog.spec: Two earlier changes each gave a borderline gain on their own and may be complementary because one adds pharmacophore information and the other removes a global physicochemical trend. Apply both in one job. (a) Build a Gobbi 2D pharmacophore fingerprint for every molecule using rdkit.Chem.Pharm2D.Generate.Gen2DFingerprint with the Gobbi_Pharm2D.factory, hash the on-bits into 4096 bins with a modulo, form a Tanimoto kernel from those bit matrices, and average it equally with the existing Morgan-Tanimoto and descriptor-RBF kernels so each contributes 1/3. (b) Before fitting the SVR, fit Ridge(alpha=10) on seven standardized physchem descriptors (MolLogP, MolWt, TPSA, NumHDonors, NumHAcceptors, NumRotatableBonds, FractionCSP3) to the rank-normalized target, subtract the ridge fit from the target, train the SVR on the residual, and add the ridge prediction back to the test molecules at the end. Keep SVR C=5.0 and epsilon=0.05.
backlog.title: Combine the Gobbi pharmacophore kernel with a physchem ridge prior

backlog.spec: train.py currently fits SVR(kernel='precomputed', C=5.0, epsilon=0.05) on a 0.5/0.5 mix of a Morgan-Tanimoto kernel and an RDKit-descriptor RBF kernel, with a rank-normalized then z-scored target. Keep everything the same but choose C and epsilon by inner cross-validation inside fit_predict instead of hard-coding them. After building K_train and the transformed target, run a 4-fold KFold(shuffle=True, random_state=seed) over the training rows, slicing the precomputed kernel with np.ix_ for each split, and score each candidate by Spearman correlation (scipy.stats.spearmanr) of out-of-fold predictions against the fold's target. Grid: C in {1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50} crossed with epsilon in {0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2}. Pick the pair with the best mean inner Spearman (ties broken by smaller C), refit a single SVR on the full training kernel with it, and predict the test kernel. This is 24 cheap fits of a 970x970 precomputed-kernel SVR per fold, so keep the grid exactly this size to stay inside the 10-minute budget; do not add any other change.
backlog.title: Inner-CV grid for SVR C and epsilon

backlog.spec: Add a featurizer that concatenates RDKit atom-pair counts (rdFingerprintGenerator.GetAtomPairGenerator(fpSize=2048), GetCountFingerprintAsNumPy) and topological-torsion counts (GetTopologicalTorsionGenerator(fpSize=2048)). Build a MinMax kernel on it (sum(min)/sum(max) via cityblock cdist as in the standard identity). Change the combined kernel to the equal-weight mean of three kernels: the existing binary Morgan Tanimoto, the existing descriptor RBF, and this new atom-pair/torsion MinMax kernel, applied identically to K_train and K_test. Leave the SVR hyperparameters and target transform unchanged.
backlog.title: Third kernel from atom-pair and torsion fingerprints

backlog.spec: The Morgan-Tanimoto kernel in train.py has most of its off-diagonal mass in a narrow band of low similarities, so the kernel is nearly flat and the SVR sees little structural contrast. Raise the Tanimoto kernel element-wise to a power p before mixing: replace tanimoto(X, X) with tanimoto(X, X) ** p and tanimoto(Xt, X) with tanimoto(Xt, X) ** p, keeping the 0.5/0.5 average with the descriptor RBF kernel and all SVR settings unchanged. Element-wise powers of a Tanimoto Gram matrix stay positive semi-definite for positive integer p, so use p = 2 as the main setting. If it is cheap to do in the same job, also evaluate p = 3 by choosing p from {1, 2, 3} with a 4-fold inner CV on the training kernel (Spearman of out-of-fold predictions, folds from KFold(shuffle=True, random_state=seed), kernel sliced with np.ix_) and refitting with the winner; otherwise just hard-code p = 2. No other change.
backlog.title: Sharpen the Tanimoto kernel with a power transform

memo: Helped: changing model family (LightGBM 0.5726, Tanimoto-kernel SVR 0.5491, from 0.6103 start), rank-normalizing the target (0.5310/0.5307, replicated), and above all averaging the Tanimoto kernel with an RDKit 2D descriptor RBF kernel (0.4830, incumbent). Did not help: FCFP (0.5877), MACCS (0.5421), stacking (0.5558), MLP ensemble (0.5500), descriptor-only ridge (0.5328), 60-descriptor subset (0.4973), autocorrelation descriptors (0.5057), RankSVM (0.5957), Laplacian solve (0.5716). Within noise (sd about 0.0070): scaffold weighting 0.4803, KernelRidge 0.4822, descriptor weighting 0.4824, extra kernels (0.4854-0.4860). Gobbi kernel (0.4680/0.4791) and ridge prior (0.4711/0.4728) were borderline gains that did not hold up on replication. Kernels look plateaued near 0.48. Next: tune SVR C, epsilon and descriptor gamma; try a GP; try quantile-transformed descriptors; maybe combine Gobbi with the ridge prior. Read train.py first, since many edits aborted by assuming a random forest or LightGBM. Replicate gains under 0.01.
